title: Trade economist explains Supreme Court decision striking down Trump tariffs
summary: Trade economist reacts to the Supreme Court tariff ruling: tariffs are paid domestically, raised prices less than feared, held back hiring, and will unwind slowly.

assertions.quote: economics has been teaching us for a hundred years that tariffs are mainly paid by domestic consumers
inflation hasn't risen as much as people expected. Prices didn't go up as much as people expected throughout the economy.

verdicts.note: Only about a quarter of a tariff reaches consumer goods prices, and the indirect channels build slowly, with marginal cost pass-through becoming significant only at nine to twelve months, so the full effect arrives over about a year rather than as a surge.

assertions.quote: they were significantly affected by tariffs and they were holding back on employment and jobs
the tariffs affected the economy was slowly and built up over time and now when we remove them it's going to slowly and build down

verdicts.note: Prices do adjust downward with a lag when tariffs truly end, but the asymmetry is larger than symmetric: price cuts come slower and smaller than the rises.

After the early-2026 tariff cut, the projected price-level effect eases over about six months, with most of the decline in the fast direct channel while the indirect effect is more persistent because U.S. producer prices adjust slowly; a projection, not observed data.

assertions.quote: the jobs report about manufacturing last year wasn't as promising as we expected and a lot of manufacturing jobs were actually lost last year

verdicts.note: BLS payroll data showed manufacturing employment declining through 2025 despite the tariffs intended to protect it.

BLS describes December 2025 as a recent low for manufacturing employment (up 72,000 since), which means the sector shed jobs through 2025, though the release does not give the January-December 2025 change.
